## Conclusion and Perspectives {#sec-conclusion}

::: {.section-subtitle}
What is proved, what is computed, and the open problems
:::

In this article, we extended our preliminary work [[QS15](#ref-QS15)] by relaxing the
unrealistic assumptions. In particular, the results hold when the durations satisfy the
triangular inequality, as well as under the assumption of [[QS15](#ref-QS15)], both of which imply
the hub triangles (H) under which they are proved. First, we defined three types of
MultiZenoTravel problem: the symmetric clique, the non-symmetric clique and the general version.

The algorithm to identify and build Pareto optimal plans relies on a single proposition. Due to
the increasing complexity of these problems, we first proved the proposition for the symmetric
problem, where the lists of $2t - p$ cities that can be flown, and how fast, are described by
admissible partitions and link forests. We then extended it to the non-symmetric version when no
flight between central cities is shorter than a detour through $C_I$ or $C_G$, the makespan of a
role configuration taking its waiting into account. Without this assumption, and for the general
version, we showed where the method of the 2023 version of this paper stops: its construction for
$B\bar A\bar B$ situations misses the Pareto front, and so does its reduction of a general instance
to a clique instance.

From an implementation point of view, we presented a version of the ZenoSolver based on an
algorithm whose number of steps is pseudo-polynomial in the durations, although computing the
makespan of a fixed list of cities is as hard as 3-Partition, a strongly NP-complete problem
[[GJ79](#ref-GJ79)]. It returns each Pareto front with a certificate, which a checker verifies
without trusting the solver; every numbered result of this paper, the checkers and a solver of
their own are formally verified in Lean 4. We demonstrated the diversity of Pareto-fronts which
can be obtained by changing the instance parameters. We validated the solver and the theory in a
seeded experiment campaign against exhaustive searches written independently of the solver.

We believe that the work presented in this paper can be useful in many regards, and in particular
for the benchmarking and comparison of algorithms, and for exploratory landscape analysis. Moreover, existing multi-objective planning instances are, as far as we know, not
offering the exact Pareto-front, which only allows the comparison between solvers but not to
characterize how hard is an instance and how far from an optimal solution the solvers are. On the
contrary, ZenoSolver is capable to return the Pareto Front, with at least one plan for each point
of the Pareto Front in the objective space.

Future work should focus on returning the entire Pareto set, i.e. all feasible plans for any
Pareto optimal objective vector. Another possible improvement would consist in characterizing the
*general* MultiZenoTravel instances for which the reduction to a *clique* MultiZenoTravel
preserves the Pareto front, and those for which it can be done in polynomial time.

### What is established {#sec-status}

The table summarises the status of the main results, from §0 of the
[theory note](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/master/doc/theory/exact-front.md). The
badge of each node says whether it is machine-checked; the [blueprint](../proofs.qmd) gives the
full status of every statement, and the [claim graph](../claimgraph.qmd) the history of each
claim.

| Setting | Pareto front characterized | Computed exactly |
|---|---|---|
| (S) and (H), so (S) and (A1), or (S) and (AΔ) | by admissible partitions ({{< node "Theorem 4.4" badge=false >}}, {{< node "Theorem 4.5" badge=false >}}) | yes, pseudo-polynomial ({{< node "Theorem 7.3" badge=false >}}), by a verified solver ({{< node "Theorem 6.9" badge=false >}}) |
| (S) only | no, a plan can beat every admissible partition ({{< node "Example 4.7" badge=false >}}) | where the lower bound $L$ meets the plans found ({{< node "Theorem 8.2" badge=false >}}) |
| Non-symmetric, (A1-NS) | by scheduled configurations ({{< node "Corollary 5.6" badge=false >}}) | bracket, then search over configurations ({{< node "Theorem 8.7" badge=false >}}) |
| Non-symmetric, (AΔ) only | not by the shuttle construction of the 2023 version ({{< node "Example 5.10" badge=false >}}); open | where the lower bound $L$ meets the plans found ({{< node "Theorem 8.7" badge=false >}}) |
| General graphs | not by the reduction of the 2023 version ({{< node "Example 5.9" badge=false >}}); open | open |

### Open problems {#sec-open}

1. **Symmetric instances without (H).** {{< node "Example 4.7" >}} shows that a plan can then
   beat every admissible partition. The relaxation $L$ remains a lower bound
   ({{< node "Lemma 3.5" >}}). The exact front is open.
2. **Non-symmetric instances with short central flights.** The shuttle construction of the 2023
   version of this paper misses the front ({{< node "Example 5.10" >}}). Open: a combinatorial
   description of the front; whether some bound on the central landings of a pattern always
   suffices; and whether flights between central cities are useless whenever $d$ and $\bar d$ order
   the cities alike.
3. **General graphs.** A characterization of the front in the spirit of
   {{< node "Corollary 5.6" >}}, with patterns that fly between central vertices from a $B$ to a
   $\bar B$, as in {{< node "Example 5.9" >}}, and costs charged by the paths actually flown; an
   exact algorithm; and the graph classes on which the reduction is exact. It fails on a path with
   two central vertices.
4. **Complexity.** Computing the makespan of a list is as hard as 3-Partition
   ({{< node "Theorem 7.1" >}}), hence strongly NP-hard [[GJ79](#ref-GJ79)], but whether deciding
   $E(T) \le C$ is NP-hard, with $t$ written in unary as in PDDL, is open.
5. **PDDL semantics.** The correspondence between PDDL plans and the plans of this paper is not
   proved, and whether planners and the validator VAL accept zero-duration actions is not checked.
   Differential tests against VAL on the emitted plans would settle the practical side.
6. **Non-symmetric gaps.** {{< node "Theorem 5.3" >}} makes the search over scheduled
   configurations exact ({{< node "Proposition 8.6" >}}); what remains is its cost, the number of
   configurations below the achieved cost at a gap, and the search over orders and matchings, which
   resembles non-preemptive open-shop scheduling.
7. **Formalisation.** Every numbered result of this paper is machine-checked. Outside Lean remain
   the hardness of 3-Partition and Partition, which is cited, the correspondence with PDDL, and the
   C++ solver, whose fronts are checked by certificates.
8. **Real-world instances.** Instances built from real data, such as the transport from Atlanta
   (ATL) to Beijing (PEK) through large intermediate airports with great-circle distances as
   durations, are non-symmetric, and they violate (A1-NS) as soon as direct flights between the
   intermediate airports are allowed: such a flight is much shorter than a detour through ATL or
   PEK. Their exact Pareto fronts are open. The plans found bound the front from above, but the
   bounds that hold for every plan, such as the relaxation of {{< node "Lemma 3.5" >}}, leave the
   gaps between them open. The data of such a benchmark, built from the OpenFlights database, is
   kept in the repository, in
   [`bench/instances/data/airports/`](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/tree/master/bench/instances/data/airports).
